response.question: Someone is selling products with my registered trademark on them. What can I do?
response.answer:
Selling products bearing your registered trade mark may amount to infringement, but it depends on the circumstances. In particular, the law covers certain unauthorised uses of an identical or deceptively similar mark on goods for which the mark is registered. Offering goods bearing the mark for sale counts as use of the mark. [trade_marks_act_1999:29]

A valid registration gives the proprietor rights in relation to the registered goods and a right to seek relief for infringement, subject to the law and any conditions on the registration. [trade_marks_act_1999:28]

However, a sale is not automatically infringement just because the products carry your mark. For example, the law provides protection in certain circumstances for resale of lawfully acquired goods that you put on the market or that were put on the market with your consent. [trade_marks_act_1999:30]

The sources available do not explain the detailed remedies or procedure for pursuing a claim.

response.question: Can I sue someone for using my brand name if I never registered it?
response.answer:
Yes, possibly. Even without registration, you may be able to bring a **passing-off** suit if someone uses the same or a deceptively similar brand name. Passing off generally concerns presenting someone’s goods or services as if they were connected with another business. The law recognises protection for an unregistered trade mark used in trade. [trade_marks_act_1999:11] [trade_marks_act_1999:134]

Whether you have a viable case depends on the facts. The sources available do not set out all the requirements for proving passing off.

A passing-off suit must be brought in a District Court with jurisdiction or a higher court. [trade_marks_act_1999:134] A court may grant an injunction—an order to stop certain conduct—and damages or an account of profits, subject to the law’s limits. An outcome is not guaranteed. response.question: Why could my trademark application be rejected?
response.answer:
A trade mark application could be refused for several reasons, including:

• The mark cannot distinguish your goods or services from someone else’s, only describes their characteristics, or consists only of terms commonly used in the trade. There is an exception if, before you applied, the mark had become distinctive through use or was well known. [trade_marks_act_1999:9]
• The mark could deceive or confuse the public, hurt religious sentiments, or contains scandalous or obscene material. Certain prohibited emblems or names can also be a reason. [trade_marks_act_1999:9]
• The mark consists only of certain shapes, such as a shape necessary to achieve a technical result. [trade_marks_act_1999:9]
• The mark is identical or similar to an earlier mark, and the goods or services are similar enough that the public is likely to be confused. [trade_marks_act_1999:11]
• Even for different goods or services, a conflict with an earlier registered mark that is well known in India can be a ground for refusal if the conditions in the law are met. Use that can be prevented under passing-off law, which can protect an unregistered mark, or copyright law can also be a ground. These grounds require an objection by the earlier mark’s owner in opposition proceedings. [trade_marks_act_1999:11]

Consent from the owner of an earlier mark or other earlier right may allow registration in special circumstances. The Registrar may also accept an application with changes or conditions rather than refuse it. If the Registrar refuses or conditionally accepts an application, the reasons must be recorded in writing. [trade_marks_act_1999:11] [trade_marks_act_1999:18]

These are general possibilities; the reason in your case depends on your mark and application.

response.question: How long is a trademark registration valid and how do I renew it?
response.answer:
A trade mark registered after the Act began is valid for 10 years and can be renewed from time to time. Each renewal lasts another 10 years from the previous expiry date. [trade_marks_act_1999:25]

To renew, the registered owner must apply to the Registrar in the prescribed manner and within the prescribed period, and pay the prescribed fee. The sources provided do not specify the form, fee amount or ordinary application deadline. [trade_marks_act_1999:25]

If the registration has expired, an application in the prescribed form with the fee and a surcharge can be made within six months of expiry. If the mark has been removed for non-payment, restoration may be possible after six months and within one year of expiry. The Registrar must be satisfied that restoration is justified and may impose conditions. [trade_marks_act_1999:25]

response.question: How long does copyright last for a book after the author dies?
response.answer:
For a book published during its author’s lifetime, copyright generally lasts for 60 years, counted from 1 January of the year after the author dies. For example, if the author died in 2020, the term runs until the end of 2080.

For a jointly authored book, the period generally runs from the year after the last surviving author dies.

Different rules can apply:
- If neither the book nor an adaptation was published before the author died, and copyright existed at death, the 60 years generally run from 1 January after first publication. If an adaptation was published in an earlier year, that earlier year is used instead.
- For a book published anonymously or under a pen name, the 60 years generally run from 1 January after first publication. If the author’s identity is disclosed before that period expires, the period instead runs from 1 January after the author’s death.

response.question: My employer says they own the articles I wrote at work. Who owns the copyright?
response.answer:
It depends on your job, the articles and your agreement with your employer.

Generally, if you wrote the articles as part of your employment, your employer is the first copyright owner unless you agreed otherwise. Being the first owner means owning the copyright when it initially arises. [copyright_act_1957:17]

There is a special rule if you were employed by a newspaper, magazine or similar periodical and wrote the articles for publication in one. Unless you agreed otherwise, the proprietor is the first owner of the rights to publish or reproduce the articles for publication in such periodicals. You are the first owner of the other copyright rights. [copyright_act_1957:17]

Copyright rights can also be assigned—that is, transferred—wholly or in part, so any agreement you made matters. [copyright_act_1957:18]

response.question: What is the jail punishment for copyright piracy?
response.answer:
For knowingly infringing copyright or helping someone else do so, the usual punishment is **six months to three years in jail**, plus a fine of ₹50,000 to ₹2 lakh. [copyright_act_1957:63]

If the infringement was not for gain in the course of trade or business, the court may impose less than six months in jail or a fine below ₹50,000. It must give adequate and special reasons in its judgment. [copyright_act_1957:63]

For a second or later conviction for the same type of offence, the usual punishment is **one to three years in jail**, plus a fine of ₹1 lakh to ₹2 lakh. A similar exception applies where the infringement was not for gain in the course of trade or business. [copyright_act_1957:63A]

A separate rule applies to knowingly using a pirated computer program: the usual punishment is seven days to three years in jail, plus a fine of ₹50,000 to ₹2 lakh. If it was not used for gain or in trade or business, the court may, for special reasons stated in its judgment, impose no jail sentence and a fine of up to ₹50,000. [copyright_act_1957:63B]

response.question: Is software patentable in India?
response.answer:
A computer programme “per se”—meaning the programme by itself—is not treated as an invention for patent purposes in India. Mathematical methods, business methods and algorithms are also excluded.

response.question: Can someone challenge or oppose my patent?
response.answer:

• After grant: An interested person can give notice of opposition to the Controller before one year expires from the date the grant was published. This includes someone engaged in or promoting research in the same field. [patents_act_1970:25; patents_act_1970:2]

response.question: Is it a crime to sell fake branded goods?
response.answer:
Yes. Selling goods with a false trade mark can be a crime. This can include goods bearing a brand’s mark, or a deceptively similar mark, applied without the brand owner’s consent.

Other defences may apply, including where the seller took all reasonable precautions and had no reason to suspect the mark was not genuine, or provided the required information about their supplier when asked by the prosecutor.

The prescribed punishment is generally six months to three years in prison and a fine of ₹50,000 to ₹2 lakh. The court may impose less than the stated minimum for special reasons recorded in its judgment. The outcome depends on the facts and any defence established.

response.question: How do I apply to register my logo as a trademark?
response.answer:
To apply to register your logo as a trade mark:

1. Apply in writing to the Registrar in the prescribed manner. You can apply for a mark you use or propose to use. [trade_marks_act_1999:18]
2. Identify the goods or services for which you want to register it. One application can cover different classes (categories), but a fee is payable for each class. [trade_marks_act_1999:18]
3. File the application at the Trade Marks Registry office for the area where your principal place of business in India is located. If you do not carry on business in India, the office is determined by your address for service in India. [trade_marks_act_1999:18]
4. The Registrar may accept the application, refuse it, or accept it with conditions or changes. [trade_marks_act_1999:18]

Your logo should be capable of distinguishing your goods or services from those of others. An earlier similar mark may also prevent registration if there is a likelihood of public confusion. [trade_marks_act_1999:9; trade_marks_act_1999:11]

If the application is accepted, the outcome also depends on whether it is opposed and, if so, how that opposition is decided. The Registrar issues a certificate when the mark is registered. [trade_marks_act_1999:23]

The available sources do not specify the application form, exact fees or full filing procedure.

response.question: What rights do I get once my patent is granted?
response.answer:
Once your patent is granted, you have rights to stop certain activities in India by others who do not have your consent:

• For a product patent, you can prevent them from making, using, offering for sale, selling or importing the product for those purposes.

As the registered patent owner, you can also grant a licence (permission to use the patent) or assign the patent (transfer it), subject to legal limits and any recorded rights of others.

These rights have limits. For example, certain uses for experiment, research or teaching are permitted. Certain government uses are also permitted. If you have co-owners, their consent is generally needed before one owner grants a licence or transfers a share, subject to applicable agreements and other provisions.

response.question: Can another company force me to let them make my patented medicine?
response.answer:
Yes, in certain circumstances. Another company cannot make you agree simply by demanding a licence, but it may apply for a compulsory licence. This is permission granted by the Controller, a patent authority, to use the patented invention. The Controller decides whether to grant it. [patents_act_1970:84]

An interested person can apply after three years from the patent grant on any of these grounds: the public’s reasonable needs are not met; the invention is not available at a reasonably affordable price; or it is not being worked in India. The Controller considers factors including whether the applicant tried unsuccessfully to obtain a licence from you on reasonable terms, although there are exceptions. [patents_act_1970:84]

When setting the licence terms, the Controller must seek to secure reasonable payment to the patent owner and a non-exclusive licence, meaning the permission is not exclusive to that company. [patents_act_1970:90]

There is also a separate route for manufacturing a patented medicine solely for export to a country with insufficient or no manufacturing capacity for that product, to address public health problems. The importing country must have granted a compulsory licence or otherwise allowed the import. The Controller grants the licence on application under specified terms. [patents_act_1970:92A]

response.question: A company copied my patented invention. What can a court order against them?

• At your choice, either damages (money for loss) or an account of profits (a remedy based on profits from infringement).

response.question: How long does copyright protection last in India?
response.answer:
Copyright duration depends on the type of work and when it was published.

• For a literary, dramatic, musical or artistic work published during the author’s lifetime, protection generally lasts for the author’s lifetime plus 60 years, counted from 1 January after the year of death. For a jointly authored work, the period is counted after the last author’s death. [copyright_act_1957:22]
• For a film or sound recording, protection lasts 60 years from 1 January after the year of publication. [copyright_act_1957:26] [copyright_act_1957:27]
• For a work published without the author’s name or under a pen name, the period is generally 60 years from 1 January after first publication. If the author’s identity is disclosed before that period expires, it is instead counted from 1 January after the year of the author’s death. [copyright_act_1957:23]
• For certain works first published after the author’s death, the 60-year period is generally counted from 1 January after first publication. An earlier publication of an adaptation can change the starting year. [copyright_act_1957:24]
• For a government work or public undertaking’s work, where that body is the first copyright owner, the period is 60 years from 1 January after first publication. [copyright_act_1957:28] [copyright_act_1957:28A]

The available sources do not establish a single rule for every possible work or situation.

response.question: How can I register my startup's brand name as a trademark in India?
response.answer:
1. Apply in writing to the Registrar in the prescribed manner. The applicant should claim to own the brand name and may apply even if it is only proposed to be used. [trade_marks_act_1999:18]

2. Identify the goods or services for which you want to use the name. You can cover different classes—categories of goods and services—in one application, with a fee for each class. [trade_marks_act_1999:18]

3. If the applicant has a principal place of business in India, file at the Trade Marks Registry office whose territorial area includes that place. [trade_marks_act_1999:18]

4. Check for earlier similar marks. A similar earlier mark covering identical or similar goods or services can prevent registration if there is a likelihood of public confusion. [trade_marks_act_1999:11]

response.question: Police officers came to my house and arrested my brother without explaining the reason. They have not allowed us to contact a lawyer or informed us about where he is being taken. What are his legal rights after arrest, and what can our family do?
response.answer:
I’m sorry your family is facing this. The information available does not establish whether your brother was arrested with or without a warrant, or what the officers told him privately. His rights include:

• Reason for arrest: If he was arrested without a warrant, the officer must promptly tell him the full details of the offence or the other grounds for arrest. [bnss_2023:47]
• Location and family contact: The person making the arrest must promptly inform a relative, friend or other person your brother names about the arrest and where he is being held. The police must also make a station-book entry recording who was informed. [bnss_2023:48]
• Lawyer: If the police interrogate him, he is entitled to meet a lawyer of his choice during questioning, although the lawyer need not be present throughout. [bnss_2023:38]
• Arrest record: The arresting officer must prepare an arrest memorandum, witnessed by a family member or a respectable local person and countersigned by your brother. [bnss_2023:36]
• Bail: If he was arrested without a warrant for an offence that is not non-bailable, the police must tell him he is entitled to release on bail and may arrange sureties—people who give an assurance for his release. [bnss_2023:47]
• Being brought before an authority: For an arrest without a warrant, the police must take or send him without unnecessary delay to a Magistrate or the officer in charge of a police station. For an arrest under a warrant, he must be brought before the required court without unnecessary delay, and the delay cannot exceed 24 hours excluding necessary travel time. The available sources do not state a maximum time for an arrest without a warrant. [bnss_2023:57; bnss_2023:78]
• When he is produced before a Magistrate, the Magistrate must check that he was informed of his contact rights at the station and that the station-book entry was made. [bnss_2023:48]

response.question: Three people attacked me while I was walking home at night. I hit one of them with a nearby object to escape, and he suffered serious injuries. Can I claim the right of private defence under Indian criminal law? Could I still be arrested?
response.answer:
I’m sorry this happened to you.

You may be able to claim private defence. The law allows you to defend your body against an offence affecting it, and something done within that right is not an offence [bns_2023:35; bns_2023:34].

Whether your claim succeeds depends on the circumstances. The right lasts while there is a reasonable fear of danger to your body [bns_2023:40]. It does not allow more harm than necessary for defence, or apply where there is time to seek protection from public authorities [bns_2023:37]. Even serious harm short of death can fall within the right, subject to those restrictions [bns_2023:39]. The fact that three people attacked you and you struck one to escape is relevant, but it does not by itself settle the claim.

Could you still be arrested? Yes, arrest is possible; a claim of private defence does not by itself settle what happened. For example, voluntarily causing grievous hurt is listed as a cognizable offence, meaning police may arrest without a warrant [bnss_2023:531]. That does not mean you will be arrested, or that the injury here necessarily meets the legal meaning of grievous hurt. The supplied sources do not set out all the conditions for arrest.

response.question: Someone posted false allegations about me on Instagram, claiming that I committed fraud. The post has damaged my reputation and affected my professional opportunities. Can I file a criminal defamation case in India? What remedies are available?
response.answer:
Yes. You may be able to bring a criminal defamation complaint about the Instagram post. The law covers published statements intended to harm someone’s reputation, or made when the person knew or had reason to believe they would do so. An allegation that lowers how others view your professional character can be relevant. Whether the offence is made out depends on the facts and any applicable exceptions. [bns_2023:356]

You can make a complaint before a Magistrate with jurisdiction. The court generally cannot take up a criminal defamation case without a complaint from the person affected. [bnss_2023:222]

The law includes exceptions. For example, it excludes a true statement made for the public good, and certain statements made in good faith to protect interests or for the public good. The court would assess any relevant exception in light of the facts. [bns_2023:356]

If the court finds the person guilty, possible punishments include simple imprisonment for up to two years, a fine, both, or community service. A fine is a punishment; it should not be assumed to be compensation paid to you. [bns_2023:356]

The available sources do not explain whether you can obtain compensation or a court order to remove the post. Ask a lawyer about those options.

A threat alone is not the capture, publication or transmission described in that section. [it_act_2000:66E]

Which provisions apply will depend on the facts. This is legal information, not legal advice.

response.question: My manager keeps making sexual comments and hinted that my promotion depends on 'being friendly' with him. Our company has about 30 employees. Where and how do I complain, and is there a time limit?
response.answer:
I’m sorry you’re dealing with this. Unwelcome sexual comments can amount to sexual harassment. A promise of favourable treatment or a threat of unfavourable treatment connected with sexual harassment may also amount to harassment. [posh_act_2013:2; posh_act_2013:3]

The workplace complaint process in the available sources applies to women. If you are a woman, you can make a written complaint to your company’s Internal Committee. Your employer must constitute one, and the order constituting it should be displayed at the workplace. [posh_act_2013:9; posh_act_2013:4; posh_act_2013:19]

If there is no Internal Committee, the complaint provision refers to the Local Committee. However, the Local Committee provision specifically mentions workplaces with fewer than ten workers and complaints against the employer. With about 30 employees, you could ask the District Officer about the appropriate route if no Internal Committee exists or if your manager is the employer. [posh_act_2013:9; posh_act_2013:6]

The usual time limit is three months from the incident, or, for a series of incidents, three months from the last incident. The relevant committee may extend this by up to another three months if it is satisfied that circumstances prevented you from complaining in time; it must record its reasons in writing. If you cannot write the complaint yourself, a committee officer or member must provide reasonable help. [posh_act_2013:9]

If you are not a woman, the available sources do not establish which workplace complaint process applies to you. A qualified lawyer can help you explore your options.

Yes. A 12-year-old is a child under the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act. Given what she has told you, report your concern to the Special Juvenile Police Unit or the local police. The reporting rule applies to any person who knows an offence has been committed or fears one is likely to be committed. [pocso_act_2012:2; pocso_act_2012:19]

If a person fails to report an offence as required, the law provides for imprisonment of up to six months, a fine, or both. This does not mean that punishment is automatic. [pocso_act_2012:21]

A person who gives information in good faith is protected from civil or criminal liability for giving that information. [pocso_act_2012:19]

response.question: I belong to a Scheduled Caste. Some people in my village insulted me using my caste name in front of everyone and are stopping my family from using the village water source. Which law protects me?
response.answer:
I’m sorry this happened to you. The Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989 may protect you in this situation.

Section 3 covers abuse of a Scheduled Caste person by caste name in public view. It also covers preventing a Scheduled Caste person from using a common water source. These provisions apply where the person responsible is not a member of a Scheduled Caste or Scheduled Tribe. Whether they apply to the people involved in your case depends on the facts.

The Act also says the State must arrange protection for victims, their dependents and witnesses against threats, violence and intimidation.

response.question: The police station near my house refused to register my FIR, saying the incident happened in another area's jurisdiction. Are they allowed to do that?
response.answer:
No—not solely because the incident happened in another area, if the information concerns a cognizable offence. You can report such an offence to the officer in charge of any police station, regardless of where it happened. [bnss_2023:173]

A cognizable offence is one for which police may arrest without a warrant. You have not described the incident, so I cannot tell whether it is cognizable; different rules apply to non-cognizable cases. [bnss_2023:2] [bnss_2023:174]

If the officer in charge refuses to record information about a cognizable offence, you may send its substance in writing by post to the Superintendent of Police (SP) concerned. If the SP is satisfied that it discloses a cognizable offence, the SP must investigate or direct a subordinate officer to investigate. If that does not happen, you may apply to a Magistrate, a judicial officer. [bnss_2023:173]

Once the information is recorded, you or the victim should receive a copy promptly and free of cost. [bnss_2023:173]

response.question: Someone cheated me of ₹2 lakh in March 2023 and I filed an FIR at that time. The trial is still going on. Does my case now fall under the new BNS or the old IPC?
response.answer:
Your March 2023 cheating case falls under the old Indian Penal Code (IPC), not the new BNS, for the alleged act in 2023. The BNS preserves penalties for offences committed under the old IPC and allows related proceedings to continue despite its repeal [bns_2023:358].

The law defining the offence is separate from the rules for conducting the trial. If your case was under investigation or trial immediately before the new criminal procedure law came into force, it continues under the old procedure code [bnss_2023:531].
